title: Is this business case tailoring appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether a way of applying or tailoring the business case practice in a scenario is effective, and pick the reason that actually explains the verdict.
question: Saltmarsh's project manager suggests that, if time runs short, the target fall in second visits may drop below the minimum the chief executive set, to protect the end date. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?

teach.h: Analyse against the guidance, not your instinct
teach.body: A BL4 business case item describes what someone did or proposes and asks whether it is appropriate, and why. Test it against three things: PRINCE2 Agile guidance (value focus, MVP, justification throughout), the products and artifacts (project brief, project canvas, benefits and sustainability approaches) and the techniques (develop, check, maintain, confirm; personas). Effective tailoring keeps the purpose and makes it lighter, more visual and more value-driven.

teach.h: How to answer a business case 'appropriate, and why?' item

steps.label: What was done?
steps.sub: Name the product, artifact or technique involved

steps.label: What does the book say?
steps.sub: Purpose and content of that product or technique

steps.label: Decide the verdict
steps.sub: Does the action serve that purpose? Yes or No

steps.label: Pick the reason
steps.sub: The one that explains THIS case, not just a true fact

rows.label: Justification
values: Business case tailored to a canvas

values: Fixed; flex Should and Could scope
Cut below minimum to save time

values: All benefits left to after closure

children.label: Not appropriate

teach.caption: Then choose the reason that names the guidance behind your verdict.

teach.body: Project manager Simon Archer makes three proposals. First, swap the council's long business case template for a project canvas reviewed at stage boundaries: appropriate, because a canvas can document the justification. Second, list 'online service launched' as a benefit: not appropriate, because that is an output; the benefit is a measurable improvement such as shorter waits. Third, measure carers' online assessments from Release 1: appropriate, because frequent releases are planned to deliver benefits early.

Typical content
Usually

teach.caption: Exactly one verdict-and-reason pair is right. A true statement is not enough: it must be the reason.

teach.text: The commonest wrong option is a true statement from the book that does not explain the case, for example 'confirming benefits mostly takes place after closure' offered as the reason a canvas update is wrong. Ask: does this reason actually decide THIS situation?

rows.label: Replace a 40-page case with a project canvas
Record 'agile transformation plan produced' as a benefit
Fix all features in the project brief to reassure the board
Plan benefit reviews after each release

items: Tailor the business case (usually into a project canvas); never remove the justification.
Benefits are measurable improvements with tolerance; outputs go under scope.
Benefits are fixed at minimum viability: flex Should and Could scope, not the minimum.
Name the MVP in the canvas; plan frequent releases for early benefits.
Pick the reason that explains the case, not merely a true statement.

summary: You can now decide whether a business case tailoring choice is effective and fit for purpose, and choose the reason that explains it. You can also reject the true-but-irrelevant reasons that most wrong options rely on.

A.q: At Callowmere University, project manager Jamal Hussain replaces the university's 30-page business case template with a project canvas, which the board reviews at each stage boundary. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a canvas can document the business justification
Yes, because a canvas removes the need to check viability
No, because a canvas is an artifact of the plans practice
No, because a canvas leaves out the costs and major risks
A.why: The project canvas is a suitable business case replacement in PRINCE2 Agile: it documents the justification from costs against benefits and value, offset by risks (Table 6.1, 6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Justification must still be checked throughout the project; the canvas is reviewed, not exempt.
whyNot.2: The canvas belongs to the business case practice (6.3.2); the release map is the plans artifact.
whyNot.3: Costs and major risks are two of the canvas's eight elements (6.3.2.1).

A.q: Saltmarsh's chief executive has said a measurable fall in second visits is the minimum improvement the board expects. The project manager proposes that, if time runs short, this target may drop below that minimum to protect the end date. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan
Yes, because benefits are flexed to protect time in agile
No, because benefits are fixed at the minimum viability level
No, because the canvas cannot change once it is approved
A.why: Table 3.1 fixes benefits at minimum viability and flexes them only above it. With time also fixed, the team should flex Should and Could scope, not the minimum benefit.

whyNot.0: True, but it does not justify cutting benefits below the minimum; scope above the Must haves flexes instead.
whyNot.1: Benefits flex above minimum viability, not below it.
whyNot.3: The canvas is a living artifact, refined and updated; that is not why the proposal fails.

A.q: Pinewick's finance director wants evidence that click and collect will increase sales rather than move them between channels. The project manager adds a canvas benefit: a net rise in total sales at live stores against comparable stores, with a tolerance. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the finance director is a member of the board
Yes, because canvas benefits should be measurable with tolerance
No, because benefits belong in the benefits management approach
No, because benefits are confirmed after closure, not planned
A.why: The canvas records expected, measurable benefits and their tolerance (6.3.2.1). A net sales rise measured against comparable stores is a measurable improvement that answers the finance director's concern.

whyNot.0: Who asked does not make the entry appropriate; its measurability does.
whyNot.2: The benefits approach covers reviews and measurement procedures, but the canvas lists the expected benefits.
whyNot.3: Benefits are planned and recorded from the start; confirmation happens later.

B.q: To reassure the Larkspur finance director, who wants a fixed list of features, the project manager writes in the project brief that every feature in all three releases is fixed scope. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board has fixed the budget and the end date
Yes, because a fixed list builds the finance director's trust
No, because the brief is produced after initiation is complete
No, because the brief should show flexible areas of scope
B.why: In agile the project brief outlines the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria based on prioritization (Table 6.1). Fixing every feature removes the flexibility that protects the fixed time and cost.

whyNot.0: True, and it is exactly why scope must flex: time and cost are fixed, so what is delivered varies.
whyNot.1: Trust matters, but it does not override the guidance that scope flexes below the Must haves.
whyNot.2: The project brief is assembled in starting up, before initiation.

B.q: Easterholm's benefits management approach plans to measure how many carers complete the online self-assessment, and their waiting times, from Release 1 onwards, with reviews at each stage boundary. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because frequent releases are planned to give early benefits
Yes, because all benefits must be confirmed before the project closes
No, because confirming benefits mostly takes place after closure
No, because measuring benefits is a task of the progress practice
B.why: In agile the benefits management approach plans frequent releases to enable early delivery of benefits, so reviewing them from Release 1 is effective (Table 6.1, 6.3.1).

whyNot.1: Most confirmation happens after closure; the point is that some benefits can be realized and reviewed early.
whyNot.2: True in general, but iterative releases can realize benefits during the project, which is why early reviews make sense.
whyNot.3: Benefits actions and reviews are defined in the benefits management approach, a business case product.

B.q: Draycott's project manager lists 'a predictive maintenance dashboard accepted by engineers' under benefits in the project canvas. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the dashboard is the main product of the project
Yes, because the canvas must name the minimum viable product
No, because the dashboard is an output, not an improvement
No, because canvas benefits must be stated as money saved
B.why: A benefit is a measurable improvement from an outcome. The dashboard is an output and belongs under scope; the benefit would be, for example, fewer breakdown hours (Glossary, 6.3.2.1).

whyNot.0: Being the main product is exactly why it is scope, not a benefit.
whyNot.1: The canvas should identify an MVP, but that does not make a product a benefit.
whyNot.3: Benefits must be measurable, which includes non-financial measures such as availability.

C.q: Larkspur's app team holds a workshop with developers, the tester and the passenger panel chair. They write four fictional personas built around needs, such as a commuter who wants compensation without paperwork. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because personas replace the need for user testing
Yes, because they are fictional, needs-based and co-written
No, because personas should be grouped by age and income
No, because the chief product owner should write them
C.why: PRINCE2 Agile advises writing personas in a cross-functional workshop with development team members, keeping them fictional and basing them on user needs; four is within the limit of five (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Personas help articulate benefits; they do not replace testing with real users.
whyNot.2: Demographics no longer predict shared needs; personas are needs-based.
whyNot.3: Co-writing in a cross-functional workshop is the advice, not a single author.

C.q: Pinewick treats Release 1, live stock levels on the website, as its MVP to test whether customers use the data. A board member asks for the MVP to be removed from the project canvas because the release map already shows Release 1. Is removing it appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the release map already shows the first release
Yes, because an MVP is an output rather than a benefit
No, because the canvas must identify the MVP for exceptions
No, because the MVP is the main benefit of the project
C.why: If an MVP is used, the canvas must identify it so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late (Table 6.1). Removing it weakens that control.

whyNot.0: The release map shows timing, but the canvas still needs to name the MVP.
whyNot.1: True, but the MVP sits in the canvas for exception control, not as a benefit.
whyNot.3: The MVP is a product, an output; it is not a benefit.

C.q: While producing Callowmere's project canvas, the project manager runs sessions comparing a single support hub with improving the existing email routes, gathering business value and benefits information for the investment decision. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because check assesses whether a project is still worthwhile
Yes, because develop explores options to inform investment
No, because benefits are confirmed after the project has closed
No, because comparing options belongs in the project brief
C.why: Develop means exploring options and getting the right information on which investment decisions can be made (6.3.1, Figure 6.3). That is exactly what the sessions do.

whyNot.0: Check is a true step, but it assesses an existing case; here options are being explored to build the case.
whyNot.2: Confirmation is mostly after closure, but that does not make exploring options wrong.
whyNot.3: Business options are one of the canvas elements (6.3.2.1).

reteach.title: Right verdict, right reason
reteach.question: Why do two people who both say 'No' sometimes get different marks?

blocks.h: The verdict is half the answer
blocks.body: Think of a referee. Two referees may both blow the whistle, but only one cites the right rule. In these items, the verdict (Yes or No) is decided by the scenario, and the reason must be the guidance that actually decides it. A true statement from a different part of the book scores nothing.

blocks.h: Business case rules that usually decide the verdict
head: Situation
Deciding rule
rows: Long template swapped for a canvas

blocks.text: Always test the reason: if you swapped it into a different scenario, would it still be true but irrelevant? Then it is the distractor.

explain.body: All projects need business justification. PRINCE2 Agile tailors the business case, typically into a project canvas, so it stays visible and easy to revisit.

test.q: Saltmarsh's board wants to replace its 25-page business case template with something lighter for Repairs Reimagined. Which reason BEST supports using a project canvas?
options: It removes the need for benefits reviews
It replaces the release map as the plan
It is owned and updated by the delivery team
It documents the justification on one page
test.why: The project canvas is a one-page visual business justification and a suitable business case replacement (6.3.2.1, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: Benefits reviews still happen, through the benefits management approach.
whyNot.1: The release map remains the plan; the canvas is the justification.
whyNot.2: The project executive leads the canvas, not the delivery team.

explain.body: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome. Products, plans and features are outputs and go under scope. Benefits are fixed at minimum viability and flexed above it.
explain.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Glossary, Table 3.1

test.q: Which item belongs under benefits in Draycott Precision Engineering's project canvas?
options: Fewer breakdown hours on covered machines
Sensors fitted to all 60 machines in both sites
A dashboard update released every week
A model trained on ten years of records
test.why: Fewer breakdown hours is a measurable improvement; the others are outputs or activities (Glossary).

whyNot.1: Fitted sensors are an output, recorded under scope.
whyNot.2: Weekly releases are a delivery pattern, not an improvement.
whyNot.3: A trained model is an output of the project.

explain.body: Because the canvas identifies the MVP, a forecast that it will be late beyond tolerance can be raised as an exception. With time and cost fixed, the response is to flex what is delivered, not the date.
explain.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 6.1, Table 3.1

test.q: Larkspur's Release 1 MVP is now forecast to miss the end of month four by more than its tolerance. Because the canvas identified the MVP, what can now happen?
options: The team adds one sprint to the date
An exception can be raised to the board
The CPO removes the MVP from the backlog
The minimum benefit can be lowered
test.why: Identifying the MVP in the canvas allows an exception to be raised if it is forecast to be late (Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance; adding a sprint breaks the fixed date.
whyNot.2: Removing the MVP would undermine the release, not control the deviation.
whyNot.3: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability (Table 3.1).

explain.body: Few (no more than five for a pilot or new product), fictional, needs-based, co-written in a cross-functional workshop. Too many shift focus and make prioritization harder.

items.label: maximum personas for a pilot or new product

test.q: Saltmarsh, using agile on a service for only the second time, is offered seven personas for the repairs journey. What should the project manager advise?
options: Keep all seven to cover every tenant
Add tenants' ages and incomes to each
Use real tenants from the panel instead
Reduce them to no more than five
test.why: For an agile pilot or new product, PRINCE2 Agile advises no more than five personas (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Too many personas shift focus and make prioritizing harder.
whyNot.1: Demographics are not the basis for personas; needs are.
